source_note: General integrated pest management principles. Not crop-specific and not yet reviewed by an agronomist. Contains no pesticide products or dosages.

prevention.action: Use healthy seed or seedlings and rotate crops.
prevention.why: Many disease-causing organisms survive on seed, soil and crop residue.

cultural.action: Remove severely affected leaves and keep the field clean of infected plant debris.
cultural.why: This lowers the source of spores or bacteria that can spread to nearby plants.

cultural.action: Avoid working in the field when plants are wet and avoid keeping leaves wet.
cultural.why: Wet leaves help many diseases spread.

mechanical.action: Take removed plant material out of the field and do not leave it lying between plants.
mechanical.why: Left on the ground it can keep infecting the crop.

biological.action: Ask an agricultural extension officer whether a suitable biological product exists for this crop and problem.
biological.why: Suitability depends on the crop, the cause and local availability.

chemical.action: Use chemical control only if a registered product is verified for this crop and problem, and follow its label.
chemical.why: Wrong products or doses can damage crops, health and the environment.

prevention.action: Check plants regularly, including the underside of leaves.
prevention.why: Finding pests early makes them easier to control.

cultural.action: Keep the field free of weeds and old crop residue that shelter pests.
cultural.why: Weeds and residue can host pests between crops.

mechanical.action: Hand-pick larvae, egg masses or heavily damaged leaves where the infestation is small.
mechanical.why: Removing pests early can stop numbers from growing.

biological.action: Avoid spraying broad-spectrum insecticides unnecessarily and ask an extension officer about natural enemies and biological options.
biological.why: Natural enemies help keep pests down and can be killed by unnecessary sprays.

chemical.action: Use chemical control only if a registered product is verified for this crop and pest, and follow its label.
chemical.why: Wrong products or doses can damage crops, health and the environment.

prevention.action: Get a soil test before deciding on fertilizer.
prevention.why: Similar leaf symptoms can have different causes.

cultural.action: Add compost, manure or crop residues to build up soil organic matter.
cultural.why: Organic matter supports nutrient supply and water holding.

chemical.action: Ask an extension officer for fertilizer type and rate based on a soil test.
chemical.why: Rates depend on soil, crop and stage; this app does not give dosages.

prevention.action: Compare the symptoms with recent weather: drought, heat, waterlogging or wind.
prevention.why: Stress symptoms can look like disease.

cultural.action: Manage water where possible: irrigate in dry periods, improve drainage after heavy rain.
cultural.why: Water stress in either direction damages crops.

prevention.action: Take a clearer photo of one affected leaf in good light, and another of the whole plant.
prevention.why: A clear image improves any AI or expert assessment.

cultural.action: Check nearby plants and note how many are affected and when it started.
cultural.why: Spread pattern helps experts tell causes apart.

chemical.action: Do not apply pesticides until the cause is confirmed by an extension officer or expert.
chemical.why: Treating the wrong cause wastes money and can cause harm.

prevention.why: Problems are easier to manage when found early.
